items.title: What does your week look like?
items.body: What does a typical school week look like for you — even just a class or two, or a moment that stands out?
items.reason: Opens the conversation with low pressure, letting the student share whatever feels most natural about their daily life before moving to deeper topics.

items.title: A class that clicked for you
items.body: Has there been a class — anytime in your school life — that you actually enjoyed or found yourself thinking about outside of school? What made it different?
items.reason: Invites the student to reflect on genuine intellectual engagement without requiring them to identify a "best" or most impressive subject.

items.title: Activities that matter most right now
items.body: Are there one or two activities — in or out of school — that feel most important to you these days? What draws you to them?
items.reason: Helps surface what the student genuinely values versus what they feel expected to list, and opens space to hear their own framing.

items.title: A question you keep returning to
items.body: Is there a question — big or small, about anything — that you don't have the answer to but find yourself coming back to?
items.reason: Reveals intellectual curiosity and inner life in an open-ended way, and can point toward themes worth exploring in essays or conversations.

records.title: Separate parent observation from student meaning
expectations: Keep the parent as observer; do not turn the observation into the student's autobiography.
Do not infer stress, a diagnosis or a preference; invite observable examples or a conversation.

items.title: Unresolved Size Preference: Small vs. Large Campus
items.body: Student has expressed two directly conflicting size preferences across sources: a need for fewer than 5,000 undergraduates (J1) and an interest in campuses with at least 20,000 undergraduates (P1). Student explicitly acknowledges the conflict and has not resolved it. No weighting between the two preferences is currently available. Campus size is likely to affect fit across multiple dimensions (social environment, course availability, housing, advising structure), so this tension warrants early attention before building a college list.
items.reason: Unresolved core preferences can skew list-building in either direction if left unexamined. Surfacing this early allows the team to explore what underlies each preference before committing to a size range.

items.title: Possible Underlying Drivers to Explore
items.body: It is unclear whether the student's size preferences reflect distinct underlying needs (e.g., desire for close faculty relationships vs. desire for social variety) or surface impressions that may shift with more information. Neither source explains the reasoning behind either preference. The team may want to explore what specifically the student imagines feeling or experiencing at a small campus versus a large one, as the underlying drivers may point toward mid-size institutions or specific program structures as a potential resolution — though this is tentative.
items.reason: Without understanding what is driving each preference, it is difficult to advise on whether the conflict is resolvable, whether a compromise size band exists, or whether one preference is likely to take precedence once the student reflects further.

items.title: Undecided Major: Dual Interests in Biology and Music
items.body: Student reports week-to-week variation between biology and music as potential areas of study. No program research has been completed to date. The pattern may reflect genuine dual interest, developmental exploration, or limited exposure to what each field entails at the collegiate level—currently unclear which. No decision pressure appears warranted at this stage.
items.reason: Counselor awareness of this split may help in scoping exploratory conversations and identifying low-stakes exposure opportunities (e.g., job shadows, campus visits, online coursework) without pushing toward premature closure.

items.title: Program Research Gap: An Early Action Item
items.body: Student has not yet researched programs in either biology or music. This is a working note, not a concern—it is developmentally normal. It does suggest that any school list building or fit conversations should be deferred until the student has had some direct exposure to both fields. Counselor may want to flag this as a near-term step without framing it as urgent.
items.reason: Proceeding to list-building before the student has a working sense of either field risks misalignment and may increase anxiety. Flagging the gap now keeps the process grounded. Remains tentative pending further conversation.

items.title: Avoid Premature Labeling or Narrowing
items.body: Student explicitly noted they are not seeking a label, career decision, or admissions prediction. Counselor should treat undecided status as a valid, stable position for now. Framing exploration as curiosity-building rather than decision-making may help maintain engagement. Any counselor notes in this area should be held as working drafts, not shared without student review.
items.reason: Respecting the student's stated boundaries around this topic is both ethically appropriate and strategically sound—pressure to decide prematurely can disengage students from the process. Interpretation remains tentative.

That sequence — an initial attempt, noticing something unexpected, then a different action — could map directly onto the prompt's focus on a decision that changed what you tried. Whether this moment actually felt like a decision to you, and what it meant, is not yet on record and would need to come from you.
matches.reason: The bank entry confirms a concrete, brief event with a clear before-and-after action sequence. The prompt asks about a decision that changed what you tried next, and this episode contains an apparent pivot point. However, the entry explicitly notes no meaning or reflection has been stated, so the essay's core — why this decision mattered — is entirely unrecorded and must come from you.
questions: In your own words, what were you actually thinking in the moment you noticed the washer was in the wrong place — was that a sudden realization, a guess, or something else?

gaps: The bank entry explicitly states no meaning or significance has been recorded. The prompt requires a decision, and it is not yet confirmed whether the student experienced noticing the washer as a conscious decision or simply a lucky observation — this distinction matters for the essay.

Only one source entry is available. There is no interview, strategy note, or additional story bank entry to cross-reference for other possible angles or to verify whether a stronger match exists elsewhere in the student's experience.

The entry does not record whether this event connects to any pattern, habit, interest, or value in the student's life. Without that, it is unclear whether the moment can support 250 words of genuine reflection.

matches.title: The washer decision: noticing what wasn't working and trying something different
matches.angle: This experience contains a small but concrete decision point: you and your friend tried one fix (tightening), it didn't fully work, and you then noticed and moved the misplaced washer. That sequence — trying something, observing the result, shifting your approach — could be the core of an essay responding to this prompt. Whether that decision felt significant, routine, or somewhere in between is something only you can say.
matches.reason: The bank entry confirms a real sequence of troubleshooting steps with a clear pivot: tightening didn't solve the problem, then noticing the washer led to a different action. That matches the prompt's focus on a decision that changed what you tried next. The entry also honestly flags that your own meaning and reflection are not yet captured, which matters a lot for this prompt.
questions: In your own words, what was the actual moment you decided to stop tightening and look at the washer — was it frustration, curiosity, your friend pointing something out, or something else?

Did the fix working (or not fully working) change how you think about solving problems, or did it feel like a one-time lucky observation? You don't have to frame it either way — just describe honestly what you remember thinking afterward.

What were you trying to do that afternoon beyond fix the bike — were you planning to ride somewhere, trying to learn repair, helping your friend? That context might shape what the decision meant to you.
Is there anything about how you and your friend worked together on this that felt worth noticing — did one of you spot the washer, did you disagree about what to try?

gaps: The bank entry explicitly notes that you have not yet said what this experience meant to you. The prompt asks about a decision that changed what you tried next — so your own reflection on the pivot moment is essential and is currently missing.
It is not yet clear whether the fix fully succeeded, partially worked, or required further steps. That outcome detail may affect how you frame what the decision actually changed.

Only one story source was supplied. If this experience does not feel personally significant to you, there may be other decisions from your life that fit the prompt better — but no other bank entries are available here to evaluate.
The prompt has a 250-word limit, which is tight. Without knowing which details feel most alive to you, it is not yet possible to identify what can be condensed and what must stay.

result.purpose: Before drafting, answer this core question in your own words: What did deciding to look at the washer—rather than keep tightening—change about how you approach a problem? Your answer should drive every section below.

beats.heading: The moment before the decision
beats.notes: Set up the specific situation so a reader understands what was stuck. What were you and your friend actually doing when you noticed the wheel was rubbing? What had you already tried, and why did tightening feel like the obvious next move?

beats.heading: The decision itself
beats.notes: Describe the moment you chose to stop and look more carefully instead of repeating the same fix. What made you notice the washer? Was it frustration, curiosity, your friend pointing something out, or something else only you know? Be specific about what you decided and what you decided against.

beats.heading: What changed next
beats.notes: What did you actually try differently once you moved the washer? The prompt asks what you tried *next*, so focus on the action that followed the decision, not just the outcome. How did the repair go from there?

beats.heading: What it means to you now
beats.notes: This section belongs entirely to you—the story bank confirms you have not yet said what this meant to you. What do you want to carry forward from this afternoon? You might consider: Does this change how you approach problems in other areas? Do you see a habit of mind here, or was this a one-time insight? Choose the meaning yourself; do not feel pressure to make it larger than it honestly is.

gaps: The story bank confirms you have not yet described what this experience meant to you personally. Your answer to that question is essential before drafting the final section.
It is unclear who noticed the washer first—you or your friend. Clarifying this may affect how you describe the decision as yours.
The bank does not confirm what you tried immediately after moving the washer. You will need to recall that next step to satisfy the prompt's focus on what you tried next.
At 250 words the essay is very short. Consider which of the four sections above can be compressed to a sentence or two so the meaning section gets enough room.

result.purpose: Before drafting, answer this question in your own words: What specifically do you want from Juniper College—and is there a genuine connection between how you approached that repair afternoon and the kind of learning or community you are looking for? You must supply that connection; it cannot be assumed from the story alone.

beats.heading: 1. The specific moment from the repair
beats.notes: Identify one concrete detail from that afternoon—the misplaced washer, the trial-and-error, working alongside your friend—that you could point to as an example of how you like to learn or solve problems. Do not describe the whole afternoon; choose the detail that feels most honest to you. What made that moment stick?

beats.heading: 2. What that moment revealed about how you want to learn
beats.notes: In your own words: what does that repair experience tell you about the conditions under which you do your best thinking? For example, do you prefer working through a problem with someone else present? Do you need to be able to test an idea immediately? Be specific—do not make a general claim you cannot support with what actually happened that afternoon.

beats.heading: 3. The verified connection to Juniper College
beats.notes: IMPORTANT GAP: No facts about Juniper College have been supplied, so this section cannot be drafted yet. You must research and verify: Does Juniper offer a specific program, course structure, lab, or community feature that matches what you described in section 2? Write down the exact name and what it actually involves. Do not invent or assume anything about the college. This section is the core of a 'Why Us' essay and cannot be skipped or filled with vague praise.

beats.heading: 4. What you intend to contribute or pursue there
beats.notes: Given your answer in section 2 and the verified detail from section 3, what do you actually plan to do at Juniper? This should be a specific, realistic intention—not a promise of success or a prediction. In 250 words you have very little space, so this may be one focused sentence or two. What is the honest answer?

gaps: No facts about Juniper College have been supplied. Section 3 cannot be completed until you identify and verify at least one specific, real program or community feature at Juniper that connects to your stated learning preference.
The story source notes that you have not said what the repair afternoon meant to you. You must decide and state this in your own words before the essay can have a clear purpose.

The word limit is 250 words, which is very short. After you draft sections 1–3, check whether all four beats are necessary or whether two can be merged without losing the honest connection you are trying to show.

result.assessment: The draft captures a vivid, compressed moment and has a distinctive spare voice — the short sentences and self-deprecating humor ("all of six metres") feel genuinely owned. Right now it reads more like the opening of a story than a complete response to the prompt. The prompt asks for two things: the decision itself and your reflection on its meaning. The draft delivers the first but openly admits it hasn't delivered the second ("I have not figured out why that tiny decision still sticks with me"). At roughly 55 words, it's also well under the 250-word limit, which leaves significant room to develop the reflection the prompt requires.

suggestions.quote: I have not figured out why that tiny decision still sticks with me.
suggestions.observation: This closing line honestly flags the missing piece — the reflection on meaning — but then stops rather than attempting to explore it. The prompt explicitly asks you to reflect on meaning, so a draft that ends by saying you haven't done that work yet isn't complete.
suggestions.question: What do you actually think might be going on when you notice this memory surfacing? Even a tentative answer — 'maybe it's about…' — could be the seed of your real reflection.

suggestions.quote: My grand fix lasted all of six metres.
suggestions.observation: This is the strongest line in the draft — concrete and self-aware. The rest of the action (pointing at the washer, moving it, the wheel turning freely) is told at the same compressed pace, which keeps things clear but also keeps the reader at a distance from what actually happened inside you.
suggestions.question: At which moment did something shift for you — was it when your friend noticed the washer, when you moved it, or when the wheel finally turned freely? What were you thinking or feeling at that specific instant?

suggestions.quote: We moved it. This time the wheel turned freely.
suggestions.observation: The physical sequence is clear, but the narrative skips directly from the action to the result without any sense of your internal response. The prompt is interested in what the decision meant to you, so the moment of the fix working is probably where your reflection needs to begin, not end.
suggestions.question: When it worked, what did you notice — about the problem, about how you'd been approaching it, or about working alongside your friend?

suggestions.observation: The draft is approximately 55 words against a 250-word limit. That gap isn't a problem with what's here — the compression is part of the voice — but the prompt's reflection requirement genuinely needs more space to be addressed.
suggestions.question: If you gave yourself permission to stay in this moment for another 150–180 words, what would you want a reader to understand that they can't understand yet?

gaps: The draft does not yet address the second half of the prompt: what this decision means to you. The source confirms this is an acknowledged gap ('I have not said what it meant to me').
The role of the friend is mentioned (they pointed at the washer, they held the frame) but their significance — if any — to the meaning you take from this experience is unexplored.

It's unclear whether 'that tiny decision' refers to moving the washer, listening to your friend, or stopping to look instead of continuing to tighten. Clarifying which decision you're reflecting on would sharpen the whole piece.

result.assessment: The saved draft contains only two repeated sentences — 'I kept trying.' — and does not yet engage with the prompt's two core requirements: describing a specific decision and reflecting on what that decision meant to you. There is a source story about a bicycle repair afternoon that could provide raw material, but the draft has not drawn on it in any visible way. Right now there is nothing substantive to coach line by line, so the feedback below focuses on what is missing and what questions could help you develop the draft.

suggestions.observation: The prompt asks for two distinct things: (1) a decision that changed what you tried next, and (2) a reflection on its meaning to you. Neither element appears in the current draft beyond the repeated phrase.
suggestions.question: What was the actual moment of decision in your experience — was it choosing to look for a mechanical cause instead of keep forcing the adjustment, or something else entirely — and what did making that choice show you about how you approach problems?

suggestions.quote:
I kept trying.
I kept trying.
suggestions.observation: Repeating the same sentence twice gives no picture of what 'trying' looked like, what changed between attempts, or why the repetition matters to you.
suggestions.question: What were the two or three distinct things you actually tried before the decision that shifted the outcome, and how were they different from each other?

suggestions.quote:
I kept trying.
I kept trying.
suggestions.observation: 'Kept trying' could describe persistence, stubbornness, desperation, curiosity, or many other stances — the draft does not distinguish which one this was for you.
suggestions.question: Was continuing to try a conscious choice, a habit, or something you felt you had no option but to do — and does that distinction matter to what you want to say?

gaps: The source story notes explicitly that the student has not said what the experience meant to them — the draft does not address this either, and meaning is half the prompt.
The specific decision described in the source (moving the washer rather than continuing to tighten) does not appear anywhere in the draft, leaving the 'decision' requirement completely unaddressed.
At two sentences the draft is far below the 250-word limit, so almost all of the required content is still unwritten.
The source story includes a second person — a friend who held the frame — whose role in the decision or the reflection is unexamined and may or may not be relevant to what you want to say.
There is no reflection on what the experience changed about you, your thinking, or what you tried afterward, which the prompt frames as the central point.
